name: Nikhil Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Nikhil. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or the government. Everything you say stays confidential, and nothing goes back to your employer with your name on it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a continuous miner at a potash mine, about a kilometre underground. It's a big machine with a spinning drum covered in picks that chews into the potash seam, and it loads straight onto a shuttle car behind me. A good shift is cutting steady, keeping the ventilation right and not hitting a soft spot in the roof. I like that it's a skilled thing, you feel the seam through the machine, and what wears me out is the rotating roster, my body never knows if it's morning or night.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You mentioned you use AI tools every day. Where do they fit?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mostly for my little side business. I bought a second-hand mini excavator two years ago and on my days off I do trenches, driveways and footings for people around town. I use AI to write quotes, work out how much a job will take, even to plan the week around my roster. Claire, my wife, says I spend more time talking to my phone than to her, which is fair on a bad week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful tool and people got too excited. Work hard, use what helps, ignore the rest. At the pub I'd say the mine still needs blokes who can feel the seam.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be a little disappointed, because I'd hoped it would help my business more. But for the family it's good, the mine job's steady and the side work keeps growing. I'm happy enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going with the mine and keep growing the excavator business on weekends. I'd use AI for the quotes and bookkeeping, maybe build a simple website for the business. Savings would keep going in, about three months now, and the excavator's nearly paid off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, but itchy to do more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much does the side business bring in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On a good month, maybe twelve hundred after fuel and the loan. On a bad month, nothing, especially in the wet. It's not big money, but it's mine, and I like being my own boss two days a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Claire think of the side business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She likes the money and hates the mud on the driveway. She's the steady one, she works at the bank in town, and she keeps me from buying a second machine every time I see a good deal. We pray about the big decisions together, and that slows me down, which is probably good.

S0.say: I'd say AI is a useful tool and people got too excited. Work hard, use what helps and ignore the rest, because the mine still needs people who can feel the seam.
S0.think: I'd be a little disappointed because I'd hoped it would help my side business more. But the mine job is steady and the side work keeps growing, so I'm happy enough.
S0.do: Keeps his mine job and grows his weekend mini excavator business, using AI for quotes, bookkeeping and a simple website. Keeps saving, with about three months put by and the excavator nearly paid off.
S0.feel: Calm and content, but itchy to do more.
S0.quote: It's not big money, but it's mine, and I like being my own boss two days a week.
S0.fieldNote: Nikhil is an entrepreneur on the side, and the plateau mildly disappoints him. His free-market values show in his pride in being his own boss. His wife and their shared faith act as a brake on his risk-taking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is how it's always been, new machines come and good workers adapt. I'd say the company should run proper apprenticeships for the new gear. I wouldn't ask the government for much, just get out of the way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's good for me. The continuous miner will get more automated, sure, but someone has to supervise it, and my business could use the same tools to win more jobs. I'd be on the right side of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put my hand up for any automation trial at the mine. In the business, I'd buy a second machine, a small loader, maybe twenty thousand second-hand, and use AI to plan jobs so I can take on more. And I'd look at the GPS machine control kits that let the excavator dig to a design, because that's more jobs in less time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, even a bit excited. Like the start of footy season.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd buy a second machine. What would Claire say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd want to see the numbers first, and fair enough. I'd show her six months of bookings and what the loader would add. If she said not yet, I'd wait, that's how we do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work might struggle with this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old Pete on the shuttle car. He's a good bloke, been here thirty years, but he still writes his roster on his hand. I'd tell him to come and work for me on weekends if the mine let him go, I'd mean it too.

S1.say: I'd say new machines always come and good workers adapt. The company should run proper apprenticeships for the new gear, and the government should mostly get out of the way.
S1.think: It's good for me: someone has to supervise the more automated continuous miner, and my business can use the same tools to win more jobs. I'd be on the right side of it.
S1.do: Volunteers for automation trials at the mine and buys a second-hand loader for about twenty thousand once his wife agrees. Looks at GPS machine control kits for the excavator to take on more work.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit excited, like the start of footy season.
S1.quote: He still writes his roster on his hand.
S1.fieldNote: Nikhil sees steady change as an opportunity and wants to automate his own business. He wants less government and more company apprenticeships, which fits his outlook. His offer to hire an older workmate shows community feeling alongside his ambition.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shock and people need to keep their heads. Look after your family, look after your neighbours. I wouldn't be out protesting, I'd be working out what to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it's a problem for my business too. If robots can dig a trench, then my little excavator business is up against companies with robot fleets. Two years isn't enough to build anything to compete.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sell the loader, or not buy it, and keep the cash. I'd probably sell the mini excavator within the first year too, before everyone else tries to sell theirs and prices crash. And I'd keep every mine shift going while it lasts and save hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Restless. I'm not one to sit still, but there'd be nowhere to run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the two-year warning do to your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It flips them. With more time, I'd own the robots. With two years, I'd be competing against them with a second-hand machine and a phone. It's the difference between being the farmer and being the horse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said look after your neighbours. What would that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our parish already does meals for families in trouble, and I'd be on the roster. If I had a skill someone needed, I'd give it. That's how a town survives, not waiting for someone in the capital to send a cheque.

S2.say: I'd say it's a shock and people need to keep their heads, look after family and neighbours. I wouldn't protest, I'd work out what to do.
S2.think: It's a problem for my business too, because robot fleets could dig trenches cheaper than my one excavator. Two years isn't enough to build anything that competes.
S2.do: Drops the loader purchase and sells the mini excavator within the first year before prices crash. Works every mine shift while it lasts and saves hard, and helps with his parish's meals roster.
S2.feel: Anxious and restless, with nowhere to run.
S2.quote: It's the difference between being the farmer and being the horse.
S2.fieldNote: The fast picture flips Nikhil's opportunity into a threat to both his job and side business. His response is quick and market-minded: sell before prices crash. He looks to parish and neighbours, not government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short, so get moving. Don't wait for anyone to save you. I'd say it to the guys at work and to my mates in town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years is just enough to get on the right side of it if I move fast. Buy the robot gear early, while it's still new and people are scared of it. I'd be one of the first small operators in town with automated machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go full time on the business in year two, if the numbers stacked up, and leave the mine. I'd buy a GPS-guided machine and then the first robot excavator I could afford, probably with a loan. Claire would have to agree, and we'd keep at least three months of savings untouched no matter what.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more excited than scared. It feels like a race I could win.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A loan for a robot excavator is a risk with a mortgage and two kids. How would you manage that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carefully. I'd only buy when I had signed jobs to cover the payments. And I'd keep the mine job until the business could pay us for six months. Claire would make sure of that, she's the bank, literally.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Arjun about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's thirteen and he loves gadgets. I'd tell him to learn how the robots work and how to run a business, both. The ones who own the machines will be all right, the ones who just use them won't.

S3.say: I'd say five years is short, so get moving and don't wait for anyone to save you. I'd tell workmates and mates in town the same.
S3.think: Five years is just enough to get on the right side of it if I move fast. I'd buy robot gear early and be one of the first small operators in town with automated machines.
S3.do: Leaves the mine in year two to run the business full time if the numbers work, and buys GPS-guided and then robot excavators with a loan backed by signed jobs. Keeps at least three months of savings untouched.
S3.feel: Uneasy but more excited than scared, like a race he could win.
S3.quote: The ones who own the machines will be all right, the ones who just use them won't.
S3.fieldNote: With five years Nikhil plans to become an owner of automation rather than a victim of it. He's careful about debt, with his wife as the check. His advice to his son captures his whole outlook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so there's no excuse. Learn, build something, look after your own. I'd say that to anyone, including my kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, ten years is a gift. I could grow the business slowly, buy robot machines as they get cheaper, and maybe hire a couple of people from the mine to run them. By the time it fully arrives, I'd want to own the machines, not be replaced by them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first couple of years I'd stay at the mine and build the business. I'd buy automated gear in about year three or four, when it's proven but not yet common. And I'd talk to Claire about setting up a fund for the kids' education, because they'll need to be flexible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. It feels like something I can plan for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're calm about AGI arriving. What if robot companies just do all the earthmoving themselves?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd find the bit they don't want, small jobs, awkward blocks, old ladies who want to talk about where the drain goes. I'm not naive, the big players might squeeze me out. But ten years is enough to find my corner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've talked a lot about owning machines. Who loses in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: People like old Pete, people who never wanted to run a business. That's where families and churches come in, and maybe businesses like mine taking someone on. I don't think a government cheque fixes that, but I know it's not enough to just say work harder.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty, so there's no excuse: learn, build something and look after your own. I'd say it to anyone, my kids included.
S4.think: Ten years is a gift: I could grow the business, buy robot machines as they get cheaper and hire people from the mine to run them. I'd want to own the machines, not be replaced by them.
S4.do: Stays at the mine for the first couple of years while building the business, then buys automated gear around year three or four. Sets up an education fund for the children with his wife.
S4.feel: Mostly calm, as if it's something he can plan for.
S4.quote: Then I'd find the bit they don't want, small jobs, awkward blocks, old ladies who want to talk about where the drain goes.
S4.fieldNote: Nikhil is calm here because ten years fits his plan to own automated machines. When pressed, he admits big firms might squeeze him and that "work harder" isn't enough for everyone. He relies on families, churches and small businesses rather than government.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: We've been through all five pictures. Of the five, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd be stuck with an old machine and a phone, competing against robot fleets. What would help is cheap loans for small businesses to buy the new gear, and less red tape to start up. And the mine giving workers a fair payout so we've got a stake to start with.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. Claire and I pray about every big decision, and it's kept me from a few silly ones. Whatever happens with the robots, I think people will need something bigger than work to hold on to.

headlineQuote: Whatever happens with the robots, I think people will need something bigger than work to hold on to.
portrait: Nikhil Dubois is a 43-year-old continuous miner operator at an underground potash mine who runs a small weekend earthmoving business with a second-hand mini excavator. He's free-market, family and faith centred, uses AI every day for his business, and makes big decisions with his wife Claire, who works at a bank. He stays calm in the milder pictures and sees steady change as an opportunity, but two-year AGI makes him anxious because he'd be competing against robot fleets with old gear. With five or ten years, he plans to own automated machines himself, while admitting that people who don't want to run businesses will need families, churches and more than "work harder".
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because he'd be stuck competing against robot fleets with an old machine and a phone.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap loans for small businesses to buy new gear, less red tape to start up, and a fair payout from the mine to give workers a stake.
